newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin stalls on giving up foreign cars.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin stalls on giving up foreign cars.

text.p: Deputy premier Boris Nemtsov's dream of forcing Russian officials to dump their foreign cars for local models was dented on Monday when Kremlin officials said they had just ordered thousands of new imported sedans.

Nemtsov, whose first act as first deputy prime minister last month was to urge the government to switch to 1970s-style Volgas from his home city of Nizhny Novgorod, insisted on Sunday his colleagues were right behind him.
But senior officials said on Monday that, despite a formal government order inspired by Nemtsov, it would be years before Volgas drove Volvos out of the Kremlin car pool.

A senior official dealing with purchasing for President Boris Yeltsin's administration told Reuters the government had recently signed firm contracts to buy thousands of foreign sedans for Moscow and top regional officials.

"We have not yet formally received the order (on switching from foreign to Russian cars), but it will not cancel contracts struck before April 1, the day the new rule came into force," the Kremlin official, who asked not to be named, said.
Under one contract, Russia would buy about 2,000 Volvo cars from Sweden for officials.

Another Kremlin official said Russian cars already made up two thirds of the government car pool. But Kommersant Daily newspaper said on Saturday the new contracts assumed most of the government's 1,450 cars would be replaced with foreign cars.
The purchasing official would not say when the latest contracts were signed.
Russian media speculated that the deals were struck after Nemtsov promised an end to flash foreign limousines and sang the praises of Volgas from Nizhny Novgorod's GAZ GAZA.RTS plant.
Nemtsov said on Sunday foreign cars would be auctioned off.
"When life is miserable for most people, it is not proper for the rulers to wallow in riches," he said last month.
"Enough riding in Mercedes and Rolls-Royces."
Yeltsin himself favours a blue Mercedes-Benz. Few if any officials drive Rolls-Royces.

But Moscow's roads are clogged with government Audis, Saabs, Volvos and Mercedes-Benz cars, jumping traffic jams of coughing Ladas and racing down special lanes once reserved for communist chiefs in frumpy Soviet ZiLs and Volgas.
Gennady Suvorov, chief aide to the head of GAZ in Nizhny Novgorod, said the plant could offer officials a customised Volga sedan for $17,420 or a basic model for $9,580.
A government delegation would visit the central Russian city next week, possibly to discuss the deal, Suvorov told Reuters.
Nemtsov, 37, says Volgas, even customised and taking into account their poorer maintenance record, would be half as expensive for the groaning federal budget, than foreign marques.
It would also create jobs in Russia, he notes.
But Kremlin officials argue that the new rule, far from saving money, would be more likely to cost more.
"We have to pay $30,000 for a tuned-up Volga, which does not meet ecological and safety norms and is much worse on the road than foreign makes," said the Kremlin official.
Presidential business manager Pavel Borodin said last month that of 700 Russian-made cars he bought for official use each year, 200 broke down immediately and 300 more within weeks.
